name: Magus

multiclassing.title: Multiclassing
paragraphs: When multiclassing into a Magus, apply the same requirements (13 Int) and proficiencies as a Wizard. You gain no extra proficiencies in skills, armor or weapons and the class functions as a full caster for the purposes of spellcasting. However, the Magus cannot be multiclassed into by a character who has levels as a Wizard and vice versa, due to functional conflicts between the two. The Magus is to be considered a Wizard of a different type, and not a separate class.

items.label: Proficiencies Gained
items.value: None beyond those granted by the standard multiclassing rules for a Wizard.

rows.features: Ability Score Increase, Arcane Studies (3rd Spell)

blocks.text: Magus are mages by blood, using magic circuits that exist within their body to channel magical energy and form it as feats of arcane wonder. Their magic uses principles that reproduce natural occurrences but reduce the time and contort the materials required. All knowledge they gain is stored within their magic crest, a special type of invisible marking that is part of their magic circuits.
See chapter 10 of the Player’s Handbook for the general rules on spellcasting.

At 1st level, you know three cantrips of your choice from the wizard spell list. You learn additional wizard cantrips of your choice at higher levels, as shown in the Cantrips Known column of the Magus table.

blocks.title: Known Spells at 1st Level and Higher

blocks.text: At 1st level, you know four first level spells from the wizard spell list.

The Spells Known column of the Magus table shows when you learn wizard spells of your choice, gain 1 new spell each time you gain a level in this class. Each of these spells must be of a level for which you have spell slots. For instance, when you reach 3rd level in this class you can learn one new spell of 1st or 2nd level.

Whenever you choose a new spell after gaining a level in this class you may also choose to switch one of your known spells out for a new one. The new spell must be of a level you can currently cast and follows the same rules as otherwise learning new spells.
You can cast a wizard spell as a ritual if that spell has the ritual tag and you have that spell in your magic crest.

Magus cannot learn spells of 7th level or higher normally. Though they gain spell slots of 7th level and higher, they cannot learn spells at those levels through their normal class features (including Arcane Studies and Magecraft). They may, however, learn higher level spells through means your DM describes or through your family crest.

Intelligence is your spellcasting ability for your wizard spells. Your use of magic comes from study and application of principles that you have poured over and made part of yourself. Not unlike scientific formulas, these traditions and methods are employed in a straight-forward pragmatic sense to achieve the desired result. You use your Intelligence when a spell refers to your spellcasting ability, and when setting the saving throw DC for wizard spells you cast and making an attack roll with one.

items: Spell save DC = 8 + your proficiency bonus + your Intelligence modifier
Spell attack modifier = your proficiency bonus + your Intelligence modifier

blocks.text: You use an arcane focus (found in chapter 5) as a spellcasting focus for your wizard spells.
Whenever a scroll, magic item, or effect calls for a wizard as part of its requirements for use, attunement, etc., the magus counts as if they were a wizard.
The spells you learn are added to your magic crest which is a part of you. It can take many different forms.

You have a certain degree of ability in regards to memorizing and casting spells you find in spellbooks, on scrolls, and in other written forms. As long as it is a wizard spell, you can spend time with such a spell to memorize and dedicate its use to memory, burning its function into your magic crest. You can only copy a number of spells this way equal to your Intelligence modifier, and to learn more like this you must unlearn one you previously learned this way and purge its knowledge from your crest.

For each level of the spell, the process takes 2 hours and costs 50 gold. The cost represents components you expend as you experiment with the spell to master it, as well as the materials required to modify and change your magic crest.

Once you have spent the time and money, you can cast the spell like any other spell you know. Unless the source you're copying from says a magus specifically can, you cannot copy spells of 7th level or higher.

A magus may choose to transfer part of their magic crest to another magus. To do so, the magus must spend the same amount of time and resources as if they were copying it. During this period, they must be in physical contact with the other magus and enter a state of meditation or synchronization with them. This period cannot be disturbed or the process fails, and neither member may sleep or engage in other activities that aren't beneficial to their rapport during this period. By transferring this part of their magic crest, the magus grants a spell they choose to the other. The other magus learns it immediately and it does not count against their Spells Known. Next time the magus gains a level and would be able to learn a new spell, they may choose to make this spell a permanent part of them in place of the new spell. When a magus transfers a spell this way there is a chance they may lose the spell themselves - equal to 5% multiplied by the level of the spell.

All magecraft that you perform is the result of mixing various amounts of the five classical elements together. Four of these elements are true energy, while the fifth is a base called void that mixes with the others to produce the result desired. If any of your features refer to your elemental affinity as per this class, they refer to one of the following classical elements which corresponds to a damage type as follows:

When you take this class, you choose one of the above elements which becomes your elemental affinity. Whenever you cast a spell that deals damage of one of your affinity types, you may use your bonus action to cast the spell as if the spell slot you used were one level higher. You cannot upcast spells this way at a level higher than your highest level spell slot.

You automatically learn the cantrip arche blast, which counts as a wizard spell for you but doesn't count against your magus cantrips known. This spell functions identically to the spell eldritch blast in all ways, except that its damage is any of the elements you are attuned to (you choose which when you cast the spell).

If you choose another element not listed above to be your affinity, choose one element from among the following: acid, cold, fire, force, lightning, necrotic, poison, psychic, radiant, thunder, slashing, piercing, bludgeoning. You gain the effects as described above for that element and also have resistance against that type of damage.

At 2nd level, you choose any arcane tradition available to a wizard, or a magus' craft focus. These define the focus of the mage's career path and their studies. The craft focuses are detailed at the end of the class features. Your arcane tradition/craft focus grants you features at 2nd level, then again at 6th, 10th, and 14th level.

Starting at 2nd level, you gain access to greater magecraft proficiencies, allowing you to manipulate your magic with greater specificity. You may choose to gain two of the magecraft features listed at the end of this class description. You can choose an additional magecraft feature when you reach 5th, 9th, 13th, and 17th level in this class.

Some of the features require ether points which you spend when you cast the spell or use that feature. You have an allotment of ether points equal to half your magus level (rounded down) + 1. You regain spent ether points whenever you finish a long rest.

Starting at 3rd level, your magic circuits allow you to apply otherwise wasted mana to the destructive power of your magecraft. Whenever you cast a spell that deals damage to a creature, and you cast it at a higher level than its base level, you can add extra damage to the spell equal to the difference between the spell's base level and the spell slot you used. If the spell can only deal damage to a single target it adds twice the difference instead.

This extra damage only applies to instant effects that resolve on the same turn the spell was cast. It does not apply to ongoing damage, damage caused by actions on subsequent turns (such as spiritual weapon or storm sphere's bonus action lightning bolt) or damage caused by weapons or targets benefiting from the spell's effects (such as a weapon enhanced by elemental weapon).

Whenever you reach 4th level, and again at 8th, 12th, 16 and 19th level, you can increase one ability score of your choice by 2, or you can increase two ability scores of your choice by 1. As normal, you can't increase ability scores above 20 using this feature.

Starting at 5th level, your studies have resulted in a deep understanding of one of the spells you have researched and perfectly memorized. Choose one spell from the wizard spell list that you have a high enough level spell slot to cast. You reserve a small amount of magical energy for this spell and can cast it once per long rest without expending a spell slot, but when you cast it this way you must cast it at its base level.

You can choose another spell to cast this way when you reach 11th and 16th level. None of the spells that you take with this feature can be 7th level or higher. These spells do not count against your magus spells known.
Whenever you cast a spell that requires a spell attack roll to deal damage, that spell attack scores a critical hit on a d20 result of 19 or 20.
Whenever you cast a spell that requires a spell attack roll to deal damage, that spell attack scores a critical hit on a d20 roll of 18, 19, or 20.
Your spellcasting has reached a phenomenal stage. Your understanding of magic allows you to scale back your inefficient mana expenditure.

When you cast a spell that you learned through a magus class feature you may treat its' base level as if it were 1 level lower (minimum 1st), allowing you to cast it with a lower level spell slot. If the spell has different effects when cast at a higher level, the spell slot level needed to meet those requirements is also lowered by 1.
Prerequisite: 9th level

Whenever you cast a spell that deals damage related to your elemental affinity you may add your Intelligence modifier to the damage roll as long as that damage requires an attack roll or saving throw, unless you were already adding it to the damage.

By regulating the flow of mana in your body and preparing certain constant defenses, you protect yourself from the effects of certain ailments. You have advantage on saving throws against effects that cause the condition you choose. Choose two of the following conditions: blinded, charmed, frightened, stunned, paralyzed, poisoned, deafened, or petrified.

Choose one of the following classes: cleric, druid, ranger, warlock. Whenever you learn a new spell after gaining a magus level (including when you take this magecraft) you can choose to take a spell off of the spell list of the class you choose in place of a magus spell. The highest level of the spell you can choose, maximum level you can cast the spell at, and number of spells from this class you can have on your spell list are all equal to half your proficiency bonus (rounded up). You cannot learn cantrips using this feature.

Whenever you cast a spell that requires concentration while already concentrating on another spell or effect you can spend an amount of ether point to concentrate on both. The amount is equal to half the level of the spell (rounded up). You roll both concentration checks as one, succeeding or failing both together. If you cast another spell and use this effect to concentrate on the new spell, you must drop concentration on one of your existing spells.
Prerequisite: 9th level

You have resistance to the damage types associated with your elemental affinity. If you already had resistance to these damage types, you take 10 fewer points of damage from effects or attacks that deal that damage type (calculated after your resistance).

Whenever you cast a spell that requires its targets make a saving throw, you may give them disadvantage on their rolls against this spell for one turn. You spend an amount of ether points equal to twice the number of creatures making saves against this spell that you would like to target. If the spell has lasting effects that require saving throws on subsequent turns, you may use an ether point each time they make a save against its effects to give them disadvantage again on that turn.

Whenever you cast a spell of 1st level or higher, you can briefly pulse your own body with magic energy. You may immediately take an extra 10 feet of movement that does not provoke opportunity attacks and ignores difficult terrain.
As a bonus action, you may touch a weapon and spend one ether point. That weapon is treated as if it were magical for 1 hour.

You learn the spell magic missile. Whenever you cast it, you may choose to cast it in a special way referred to as gandr shot. When you cast it this way, you must make an attack roll for each missile you fire (one roll per target) and the damage is increased to 5 (1d6 + 1) force damage per missile. Any creature you hit with a gandr shot must attempt a Constitution saving throw. On a failed save they are poisoned until the start of your next turn.
Prerequisite: 9th level
Whenever you cast the spell mage armor you can choose to calculate your Armor Class as 10 + your proficiency bonus + your Dexterity modifier instead.

By flooding your body with magical energy you can reduce the effects of other magic against you. As a reaction to being targeted by a spell effect that requires a saving throw or attack roll you may spend 1 ether point. If you do: you gain advantage on all saving throws against spells, and magic effects and spell attacks that target you have disadvantage until the start of your next turn.
Prerequisite: 9th level

When you cast a 1st level or higher spell for the first time on your turn, you may spend any number of ether points as a bonus action. You may immediately cast a second 1st level or higher spell of a level equal to the amount of ether points you spent, but cannot cast any other spells after it until the start of your next turn (including reactions). The spell cast this way cannot be a higher level than your Intelligence modifier.

Whenever you cast a spell that target a single creature and requires an attack roll to hit and deal damage, you may spend a number of ether points to add extra damage to the spell's initial damage, equaling 1d6 damage per ether point spent this way. You cannot spend more ether points than the level the spell is cast at.

Whenever creatures attempt to use spells like dispel magic or counterspell against your spell effects, they must roll against the level of your magical effect to determine if they should succeed even if it would normally succeed automatically.
Whenever you roll an attack roll, ability check, or Dexterity saving throw you can spend 1 ether point to roll 1d6 and add it to the result.

items.label: Hit Points at Higher Levels
items.value: 1d6 (or 4) + your Constitution modifier per Magus level after 1st

items.label: Skills
items.value: Choose 2 from Arcana, History, Insight, Medicine, Nature, Persuasion. Also proficient in Deception

blocks.text: You start with the following equipment, in addition to the equipment granted by your background:

items: (a) a component pouch or (b) an arcane focus

blocks.text: You may instead choose to start with gold equal to 40 (4d4 × 10) gp.

introduction: Magus, known also as mages and magi, are those who utilize magecraft to perform things that many would call miracles. By combining elemental energy with ether clumps they generate effects that replicate those in nature. Not unlike science, but certainly separate from it: it achieves results comparable to science and natural processes by inputting energy and different types of theory. This is the essence of magecraft.

Usually cordial and compliant with other mages, the magus is ultimately self-serving. What may seem to be a well-meaning aristocrat on the surface could in fact torture undeserving victims below their home in a secret dungeon, rationalizing this behavior as a means of studying to discover greater mysteries. However, for each mage like that there is one that believes in decorum and is an upstanding individual who won't stand for injustices. Magus believe that, because the natural laws of the world do not apply to them, it is of the highest importance that they obey the laws they set out for themselves.

Unlike other types of spellcasters, they have powerful magic circuits merged with their nerves which allows them to convert internal energy into a highly efficient form. This powers their magecraft, which can seem destructive or flashy compared to many other mages.

lore_sections.title: Pursuers of Truth
paragraphs: The ultimate goal of all magi is to reach Truth in the form of reaching the Root. At the source of everything, the Root exists "outside" the world as we know it. To reach it would mean an escape from the limitations of the "inside" of the world and liberation from its oppressive laws. Very few have ever reached the Root, but those who did returned with access to true miracles known as True Magic. Only five exist, and the path they took to the Root cannot be retread, so only new True Magics can be discovered. This is the final goal of all magus, and those who reach this level of magic are known as magicians. Only a handful of mages exist with this illustrious title.

In an effort to reach the Root, mage clans try many things. They explore the soul, the stars, the world, and more. There is no sure path. Knowing that one generation will not be able to accomplish this alone, mages pass their legacy exclusively to their successors. They store their knowledge and progress in a family crest: a portion of magic circuits passed from family head to family head, allowing the next in line to pick up where they left off. Each magus that accepts the work of their forebears must confront the question that will define their life: "what am I going to add to all this?"

lore_sections.title: Secretive Scholars
paragraphs: Magic functions like a program that draws upon the Root. Each spell was once much more powerful, but as their mystery was peeled away and spells became known by more and more mages, the spells became weaker and unfocused. The only magic untouched by this is True Magic, remaining exclusive and unaffected in its power. For these reasons magi keep their work secret and strive to find new paths rather than retread the obvious. The more innovative a mage can be the greater the result. New secrets yield better results than old secrets by a great deal.

This expectation that a mage family will be secretive has led to some internal contradictions that enable certain horrific actions. A mage that captures and experiments on uninvolved humans will be overlooked until their crimes are entirely too obvious. Many mages get away with slaughter before they are ever even considered out of place. Though these tendencies are looked down upon, it is considered in poor taste to involve the privacy of another clan's work without a strong reason.

The ultimate concern a mage has is also that of the modern public. Mages have kept their society and work secret from the world since the middle ages in an effort to curb the decline of magecraft through public knowledge. As the world progressed, a greater divide emerged in the form of advanced technology, which magi avoided. It is the belief of traditional mages that modern technology weakens and dilutes magecraft by making aspects of its core principles obsolete. If a mage is exposed to the public, it is their duty to erase the memories of those who know, or kill them. Likewise, if a mage intentionally becomes a threat to the secrecy of magecraft, other mages will take it upon themselves to eliminate them.

lore_sections.title: Creating a Magus
paragraphs: When creating your magus character you need to mostly consider what the goal of their family is. How far back does their clan go? If it reaches back ten generations then their life is likely one filled to the brim with responsibility and constant reminders of the work they carry. If it is new, that is to say only several generations old, they may be more understanding of modern ideas and have more progressive views. Some families don't find their true calling for several generations and so do not directly search for the Root, whereas some older families obsess over it. Just as well, many mage clans don't care either way and instead are concerned with the material world around them. You should consider the environment your character grew up in and what motivations they were exposed to as a result.

Furthermore, what is your character's path? If they wish to push their clan forward, what sort of direction do they want to move in? Do they believe that more powerful magic will yield status, or are they looking at finding truth in tranquility or internal harmony? There are mages who are walking incinerators and others with a distinct purity of mind. Both are equal. Where do you stand? You would know that your life must be sharpened like a knife, with your efforts pointed toward an unfaltering goal. To deviate from it is to make waste of the work of those who came before you. So what path do you walk, and what methods do you have for taking steps along it?

lore_sections.title: The Magus in Regular D&D
paragraphs: The magus is very easy to incorporate into regular settings, so long as your table would allow it. Though magic functions differently in the realms, you can simply consider magic circuits and thaumaturgical studies to be a different means by which to utilize power from the weave. Magus would seem like a half-way point between sorcerers and wizards; they have innate magical energies within their own body that they can call up when needed, and many would have innate magical powers. However they still learn spells and can treat their magic as a sort of science. "Magecraft" would then simply be the specific type of arcane techniques they use to give shape to their magic. Family crests need little alteration, but should be considered something that only those with magic circuits can utilize.

The main difference would be the behavior of magus in the world. They would not need to be as secretive, since magic is abundant. However there are some ways to add fun elements to your character and their story while preserving this tone: the Mage's Association may be an organization specifically run by magus, those who utilize this specific sort of arcane art. Furthermore, secrecy about their practices may be necessary because the arcane power they draw on may still function similarly to how magecraft degrades in the Typemoon universe: the more people know about your magecraft the weaker it may become. Magus can then act as mages who seek privacy, and perhaps can even still strive toward a metaphysical extra-dimensional storehouse of information like The Root.

You may wish to remove the limitation on 7th level and higher spells, but I actually recommend keeping this in place. It is accounted for by other features and the magus has other benefits that help it function despite it. Just as warlocks and paladins have limited spell uses and levels, the altered spell list is just one part of the identity of this class.

lore_sections.title: Magus and Wizard Overlap
paragraphs: Any item that specifies it requires a Wizard to use it, interact with it, attune to it, etc treats the Magus as if they were a wizard.

roleplay.quick_build:
The magus is very similar in many ways to the wizard, to the point of sharing subclasses. You can use the following instructions to build one quickly. First, you should have Intelligence as your highest score as it determines your spellcasting attack and save efficiency. Next, Wisdom or Dexterity. Some magus are more martial than others, whereas many are academics. If you plan to be an enforcer or martial magecraft user go with Dexterity, but in any other case choose Wisdom. Finally, take the cloistered scholar background, representing your studies at whatever magical institute you favor (likely Clock Tower).

If your DM is willing to allow it, you should be able to use any wizard subclass you wish in place of a magus subclass. Be sure to carefully consider if any of the features wouldn't work properly with the features of the magus, but regular subclasses from the core rulebooks should be fine.
